body_html:
You can build interactive sites and dashboards right inside a normal Claude chat - just describe what you want and attach your data. They look great and you can edit them by chatting. But two things make them hard to use with a team:

Caveat 1 - Not shareable
The site link only works for you. Coworkers can't open it.
Caveat 2 - Version sprawl
Every edit produces a brand-new file and a new link, so you juggle dozens of versions.

The fix is to host the HTML as a proper website. Once it lives on GitHub and Vercel, it has one stable public URL you can share, and you edit that same site through Claude Code - no more version pile-up.

title_html: How it works, at a glance
body_html:
The whole pipeline in five moves. Steps 1-7 get you a live, editable site; steps 8-10 are optional upgrades.

✷
1. Build in Claude
Chat with Claude, download the dashboard as index.html.
→
🐙
2-4. GitHub
Create a repo and upload the file.
→
▲
5. Vercel
Import the repo and deploy to a live URL.
→
💬
6-7. Claude Code
Connect the repo and edit by chatting.
Optional add-ons → 8. Neon Postgres so data edits save 9. A passcode to lock the site 10. A Dashboard Hub home button in the header
Tip: use the numbered menu on the left to jump between steps at any time.

In a regular Claude chat, describe the site you want and attach any source data (a spreadsheet, PDF, or notes). Don't overthink it - everything can be edited later, so it's better to start and refine. The more context you give Claude up front, the better the first draft. It never hurts to overshare.

Prompt builderFill in the blanks → copy your ready-made prompt
What should users be able to do?
Your generated prompt

  




Here's a real example - a loan database for a commercial real estate company:



Two things that matter. Always ask for the site as a single HTML file named index.html. When Claude gives you the file, download it - if it came down under any other name, rename it to index.html before moving on.

GitHub is where your file will live. Go to github.com and sign up using the same email address connected to your Claude account - this keeps everything linked cleanly. You only do this once.

Once signed in, start a new repository (a "repo" is just a project folder):

  1. 1
    Click the + button in the top-right corner of GitHub.
  2. 2
    Choose New repository from the menu.

Fill out the new-repository form. Most settings stay at their defaults - here's exactly what to do:

  1. 1
    Repository name - give it a clear name specific to the project (e.g. Triangle-Loan-Database). Leave Description blank.
  2. 2
    Visibility - set to Public.
  3. 3
    Leave Add README off, .gitignore on “None”, and license on “None”, then click Create repository.
A note on Public. Public means anyone who finds the repo can read its code. That's fine for most dashboards and keeps this simple - but if you add a passcode (Step 9), the lock protects the live site, not the source on GitHub. Keep genuinely sensitive data out of a public repo, or put it behind a database instead.

Turn off notifications for this repo

GitHub automatically watches every repo you create, so from this point on you'd otherwise get an email for every push, comment, and Actions run. Turn that off now, before it starts:

  1. 1
    On the repo page, click the Watch dropdown (top right, next to Fork and Star).
  2. 2
    Choose Ignore. GitHub stops emailing and notifying you about this repo entirely.

On the repo's landing page, find the “Quick setup” panel:

  1. 1
    Click the “uploading an existing file” link.

Drag in (or choose) the index.html file you downloaded from Claude, then commit it:

  1. 1
    With index.html added, click the green Commit changes button.

Vercel takes your GitHub file and publishes it as a real website. Go to vercel.com and sign up with the “Continue with GitHub” option - this links Vercel to GitHub automatically. When GitHub asks, click Authorize Vercel. (Account creation is one-time; the deploy below repeats per project.)

Start a new project

  1. 1
    In the top-right corner, click Add New.
  2. 2
    Choose Project.

Import your repository

  1. 1
    Under Import Git Repository, find your project and click Import.

Deploy

Nothing on the next screen needs to change - the defaults are correct for a plain HTML site.

  1. 1
    Click Deploy, then Continue to Dashboard once it finishes.

Grab your shareable link

Your live URL lives under Domains on the project's overview page.

  1. 1
    Copy the link under Domains (e.g. triangle-loan-database.vercel.app) - this is what you share.
  2. 2
    Visit opens the live site in a new tab.

By default Vercel emails you on every deployment, which gets noisy fast. Two quick settings fix it - one is per project, the other is once per account.

Per project - turn off pull-request comments

  1. 1
    In the project, open the Find search bar, type git, and open Git (Settings).
  1. 1
    Toggle Pull Request Comments off.

Once per account - turn off deployment emails

  1. 1
    In the Find bar, type notifications and open My Notifications.
  1. 1
    Uncheck every box in the Email column for the deployment notifications.

title_html: Connect the site to Claude Code
body_html:
This is how you keep editing the live site by chatting - no more downloading files. You connect your GitHub account to Claude Code once; after that, editing any project is just picking its repo.

You only need to connect GitHub - not Vercel. Vercel is already watching your GitHub repo and will automatically redeploy the live site whenever changes are merged. Just connect the GitHub account that owns the repo.

Open Claude Code

  1. 1
    Open Code at the top of the Claude app.
  2. 2
    Click New to start a session.

Connect your GitHub account (one time)

  1. 1
    In the message box, click the + button and choose Connectors.
  2. 2
    Click Manage connectors.
  1. 1
    Make sure GitHub Integration shows as connected (a checkmark). If it isn't, click Connect and authorize GitHub - sign in with the account that owns your repo, then choose which repositories Claude can access (all of them, or just the ones you pick).
  2. 2
    Leave Vercel unconnected - Claude Code doesn't need it. As long as GitHub is connected, you're set.

Pick your repo and edit

  1. 1
    Back in a new Code session, select the repository for this project (e.g. Triangle-Loan-Database) and the main branch.
  1. 2
    Describe your change in plain language - then publish it (see the habit below).
The one habit to remember. At the end of each edit, tell Claude Code: “Open a PR and merge to main.” That's what publishes your change - Vercel redeploys the live site automatically within a minute.

That's the core workflow. You now have a live link to share and a site you can edit anytime through Claude Code. The last three steps are optional upgrades.

title_html: Add a database so edits saveOptional
body_html:
A plain HTML site can't remember changes - if you or a coworker edit a value on the live site, it resets on refresh because there's nowhere to store it. Adding a database (Neon Postgres, free) makes edits stick for everyone. Do this if your dashboard is something people will actively update, not just read.

Create the database in Vercel

Open the project from your Vercel Overview, then find Storage in the left sidebar.

  1. 1
    On the Storage page, click Create Database.
  1. 1
    Choose Neon - Serverless Postgres.
  2. 2
    Click Continue, stay on the free plan, give it a project-specific name (e.g. Triangle-Loan-Database-DB), and create it.

Wire it up through Claude Code

Back in the Claude Code session connected to this project's repo, paste the prompt below. Vercel has already added the database's connection details to the project, so Claude Code can build against them.

Prompt for Claude Code 
I've connected a Neon Postgres database to this Vercel project (Storage integration), so DATABASE_URL / POSTGRES_URL etc. are already set as environment variables. Please refactor this site so its data is stored in and read from that database instead of being hard-coded in the HTML/JS.

Specifically:
- Database: Design whatever table(s) fit this data. If the records have a long tail of optional/inconsistent fields, prefer a simple id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY + data JSONB table over a wide column schema - it keeps every field intact without a sprawling, mostly-null schema. If the data is uniform and clearly relational, use normal typed columns instead.
- Self-healing setup - this is important: Don't rely on me remembering to run a migration/seed script by hand against the real production database. Instead, have the data-access code itself check on first use whether the table exists and is empty, and if so, create it and load the seed data automatically, before serving any request. Only seed when the table is completely empty, so it can never overwrite real edits once real data exists. (Last time I did this without this step, the live site deployed before the table existed in the real database, and it looked exactly like all the data had been deleted - don't repeat that.)
- Still include a standalone scripts/migrate.js and scripts/seed.js (or equivalent) for manual/local use - just don't make the live site depend on someone running them.
- API: Add serverless functions (in /api, or wired into the existing server if there's already a single catch-all function / auth gate) with GET to load records and POST/PUT/DELETE to create, edit, and remove them. Read the Postgres connection string only from environment variables - never hard-code credentials. If the site has an existing login/passcode gate, make sure the new API routes sit behind it too, not in front of or beside it.
- Front end: Update it to fetch from these API endpoints on page load, and save any add/edit/delete actions back through the API, so changes persist across refreshes and are visible to everyone who visits - instead of only existing in a hard-coded array or local state.
- Keep the existing look, layout, and functionality exactly the same; only add the minimal UI needed to actually create/edit/delete records if none exists yet.
- Test it end-to-end before calling it done - spin up a local Postgres, run your migrate/seed, and actually exercise GET/POST/PUT/DELETE (and the self-healing path against a completely fresh/empty database) before pushing.

When you're done, open a PR and merge to main.

Since the live URL is public, add a passcode if the dashboard shouldn't be open to anyone with the link. This adds a simple login screen in front of the site.

Doing this earlier? You can add the PASSCODE variable back in Step 5, in the Environment Variables section of the deploy screen - it's the same variable. Either way, the passcode does nothing on its own: it only becomes a working login screen once you've connected the repo to Claude Code (Step 7) and run the prompt below.

Add the passcode in Vercel

In your project, open the Environment Variables tab in the left sidebar.

  1. 1
    Open Environment Variables from the sidebar.
  2. 2
    Click Add Environment Variable.
  1. 1
    Set the Key to exactly PASSCODE.
  2. 2
    Set the Value to whatever password you want.
  3. 3
    Click Save.

Build the login screen through Claude Code

In the Claude Code session for this project, paste this prompt. It reads the passcode securely on the server, so the actual value is never exposed in the site's code.

Prompt for Claude Code 
I've added an environment variable named PASSCODE to this Vercel project (a secret value). Please add a simple password gate so the site isn't publicly viewable without it.

- Show a login screen that asks the visitor to enter a passcode before the dashboard loads.
- Verify the entered passcode against the PASSCODE environment variable on the SERVER side, via a Vercel serverless function in /api. Never expose the actual passcode in the front-end code or send it to the browser.
- If it's correct, grant access (set a session cookie/token) and show the dashboard; if it's wrong, show an error and reveal nothing.
- Keep the visitor signed in for the session so they don't re-enter it on every page load.

When you're done, open a PR and merge to main.
Order tip. You can add the passcode (or the database) at any point - before or after sharing the link. If you add it later, just remember to send coworkers the passcode too.

title_html: Add a Dashboard Hub home buttonOptional
body_html:
Every dashboard the team builds already links out from the central Dashboard Hub - but once someone is a few clicks deep inside one specific dashboard, there's no way back except the browser's back button. Add a small "Dashboard Hub" button to the header so there's always a one-click way home, no matter which dashboard someone is looking at.

Every dashboard's header looks different. That's exactly why this is step 10 and optional rather than a fixed template: some headers already have several buttons (Portfolio, Add Property, Log out…), others are bare. There's no single correct pixel position - just add a small, clearly-labeled button wherever it fits naturally among whatever's already there, usually on the opposite side from the logo/title.
▲Deal PipelineYour Company
⌂ Dashboard Hub Portfolio + Add Property Log out
Illustrative example - the new button (highlighted) sitting among a header's other existing buttons. Your dashboard's real header may look nothing like this one; the button just needs to fit in wherever its own buttons already live.

What "done" looks like

  1. 1
    A "Dashboard Hub" button (with a home icon) sits in the header on every page, styled to match that dashboard's own existing buttons.
  2. 2
    Clicking it opens https://dashboard-hub-one-vert.vercel.app/.
  3. 3
    Clicking the company logo in the header (e.g. the Triangle logo) does the exact same thing - it's a second way home, not a separate link.

Add it through Claude Code

In the Claude Code session connected to this specific dashboard's repo, paste the prompt below. It's written to let Claude find the right spot in that dashboard's own header, instead of forcing every site into the same layout.

Prompt for Claude Code 
Add a "Dashboard Hub" home button to this site's header, and make the logo do the same thing.

- Add a small button/pill in the header labeled "Dashboard Hub" (with a home icon) that links to https://dashboard-hub-one-vert.vercel.app/
- Also make the existing company logo/wordmark in the header link to that same URL, so clicking it takes you to the same place as the new button.
- Both should navigate in the same tab/window, the same way this site's other internal links already behave - not open a new tab.
- Match this dashboard's existing header style: reuse its current button shapes, spacing, colors, and font rather than introducing a new visual style. Look at where its other header buttons/links already sit and place the new button wherever it fits most naturally alongside them - every dashboard's header is laid out a little differently, so don't force one exact position or copy another dashboard's placement.
- Leave everything else in the header and page exactly as it is now - this should be a small, additive change.

When you're done, open a PR and merge to main.
Do this once per dashboard. Since each site is its own repo, repeat this Claude Code prompt separately for every dashboard the team wants linked back to the hub - the header will look different each time, so the button's exact spot (and the logo it attaches to) will too, which is expected.

The everyday editing loop

Once a site is set up, your day-to-day is just: open the Claude Code session for that repo → describe the change → end with “Open a PR and merge to main” → Vercel redeploys automatically. The shared link never changes.

Good habits

Always name the file index.html. Over-share context and data with Claude when building - it's easier to trim than to add. Give each repo and database a clear, project-specific name. And keep sensitive data out of public repos.

Which optional steps do I need?

Read-only dashboard? Steps 1-7 are enough. People will edit the data? Add Step 8 (database). Shouldn't be public? Add Step 9 (passcode). Part of a multi-dashboard team? Add Step 10 (Dashboard Hub button).
Internal walkthrough · Building shareable, editable dashboards with Claude, GitHub & Vercel. Screenshots are examples from the Triangle-Loan-Database project.
